item.title: Meta signs 6-gigawatt AI chip deal with AMD
item.description:
Meta Platforms and AMD on Tuesday announced a multi-year, multi-generation agreement to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPUs for Meta's AI infrastructure, in a deal that could generate tens of billions of dollars in revenue for the chipmaker and reshape the competitive landscape of the AI hardware market.

The partnership marks Meta's most direct move yet to diversify its AI compute supply chain beyond Nvidia, which secured its own sweeping deal with Meta just one week earlier. Under the agreement, AMD issued Meta a performance-based warrant for up to 160 million shares of AMD common stock — roughly 10% of the company — structured to vest as shipment milestones and stock price thresholds are achieved.

item.title: U.S. details alleged secret Chinese nuclear test, urges disarmament talks
item.description: A senior American arms control official on Monday presented newly declassified details of what Washington says was a secret Chinese underground nuclear test conducted in 2020, urging the international community to pressure Beijing and Moscow toward nuclear disarmament just weeks after the last remaining U.S.-Russia arms treaty expired.

item.title: King's College London creates first-ever aluminum compound to rival platinum catalysts
item.description:
Chemists at King's College London have isolated a new form of aluminum that could offer a cheaper and more sustainable alternative to precious metals widely used in industrial catalysis. The work, led by Dr. Clare Bakewell, a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Chemistry, describes the first-ever cyclotrialumane — a compound made of three aluminum atoms arranged in a triangular structure — capable of breaking apart tough chemical bonds.

Published in Nature Communications, the research comes at a time when supply chain disruptions and soaring costs for precious metals like platinum and palladium are forcing the chemical industry to search for abundant alternatives.

item.title: US and NATO launch major Arctic exercises amid rising tensions
item.description: The Arctic has emerged as a theater of intensifying military competition and environmental upheaval, with NATO launching new operations, the United States conducting exercises spanning Alaska and Greenland, and Russia and China deepening their joint presence across the region — all as record-breaking warmth reshapes the polar landscape.

item.title: Russia opens criminal case against Telegram's Durov
item.description:
Russia has launched a criminal investigation into Pavel Durov, the founder and chief executive of Telegram, on charges of facilitating terrorist activities, the state-run newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta reported on Tuesday, citing evidence from the Federal Security Service (FSB). The move marks a sharp escalation in Moscow's increasingly confrontational campaign against the messaging platform and its Dubai-based founder.

"The actions of the head of Telegram, P. Durov, are being investigated as part of a criminal case on the grounds of a crime under Part 1.1 of Article 205.1 (assistance to terrorist activities) of the Criminal Code of Russia," Rossiyskaya Gazeta reported in an article it said was "based on materials from the FSB of Russia." The charge carries a potential sentence of eight years to life imprisonment.

Durov responded to the announcement on his Telegram channel. "Russia has opened a criminal case against me for aiding terrorism," he wrote, describing the investigation as pressure on the messenger service.

item.title: Russia losing troops faster than it can replace them, Western officials say
item.description:
On the fourth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Western officials disclosed that Moscow's battlefield losses have outpaced its ability to recruit replacements for three consecutive months, a development that could reshape the trajectory of the conflict.

Since November, Russian forces have suffered nearly 40,000 casualties per month while managing to enlist only about 35,000 new troops, according to Western officials cited by The Telegraph. The growing deficit marks what analysts describe as a potential turning point in Europe's largest land war since 1945.

item.title: US warned Ukraine over strikes that hit American oil interests
item.description: Ukraine's ambassador to the United States disclosed on Tuesday that Washington delivered a formal diplomatic complaint after Ukrainian attacks on the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk damaged infrastructure tied to American oil investments in Kazakhstan, underscoring the complex intersection of the war with global energy interests.

item.title: Russia accuses UK and France of plotting to arm Ukraine with nukes
item.description:
Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service on Tuesday accused Britain and France of secretly working to supply Ukraine with nuclear weapons, an allegation that drew swift denials from London, Paris, and Kyiv and prompted one of Moscow's most explicit nuclear threats since the full-scale invasion began four years ago.

The SVR, Russia's primary foreign intelligence agency, issued the claims on the fourth anniversary of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, asserting that London and Paris "are preparing to arm Kyiv with a nuclear bomb" because they believe conventional forces cannot defeat Russia. The agency provided no evidence to support its allegations.

item.title: Bitcoin miners liquidate reserves, pivot to AI as prices plunge
item.description:
Bitcoin has fallen more than 26% year-to-date, logging its worst start to a year on record and its weakest consecutive monthly performance since the 2022 crypto winter. The decline, compounded by President Donald Trump's announcement of a 15% global tariff on imports that took effect February 24, has pushed mining operations to breakeven or below, forcing companies across the sector to liquidate reserves and accelerate their pivot away from cryptocurrency.

The original cryptocurrency dropped below $65,000 on Monday after Trump's tariff announcement over the weekend sent shockwaves through global markets, according to CNBC. Bitcoin has now posted six consecutive negative weekly closes — a first in its history — and has fallen roughly 47% from its all-time high near $126,000 set in October.

item.title: Mexico probes cartel-linked accounts spreading fake news after El Mencho killing
item.description:
When the Mexican army killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes — the fugitive cartel leader known as "El Mencho" — during a military operation in Tapalpa, Jalisco, on Sunday, February 22, genuine violence rippled across western Mexico. But researchers say a coordinated propaganda campaign by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel simultaneously manufactured a far more apocalyptic picture online, flooding social media with fabricated images and false reports designed to amplify fear and undermine confidence in the Mexican government.

Among the debunked claims: assassins had seized Guadalajara's airport, a plane was ablaze on the runway, smoke was billowing from a church and buildings in Puerto Vallarta, American tourists were being held hostage, and armed groups had attacked civilians at the airport. The Mexico Embassy in the United States issued a point-by-point rebuttal on X, labeling each claim false. A fact-check by Lead Stories found that the viral image of a burning aircraft was almost certainly generated by artificial intelligence, with the Hive Moderation detection tool rating it 93.2 percent likely to be AI-created. Telltale signs included gibberish text on boarding stairs, mismatched aircraft windows, and a figure standing implausibly close to the flames.

item.title: Gold tops $5,200 as new U.S. tariffs take effect amid trade chaos
item.description: Gold prices climbed to a three-week high this week as investors poured into safe-haven assets following a sudden upheaval in U.S. trade policy. The rally was triggered by the Supreme Court's decision on Friday to strike down President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs, and then his rapid imposition of new levies under a different legal authority, injecting fresh uncertainty into global markets.

item.title: HSBC's 2025 profit beats estimates despite $5B in charges
item.description:
HSBC, Europe's largest bank, on Wednesday reported annual pretax profit of $29.9 billion for 2025, a 7.4 percent decline from $32.3 billion the previous year, as nearly $5 billion in one-off charges weighed on results. The figure nonetheless exceeded the $28.9 billion analyst consensus compiled by Bloomberg, buoyed by strong performance in wealth management and transaction banking.

"2025 was a year of decisive action and swift execution, which is reflected in our strong performance," Group CEO Georges Elhedery said in the bank's earnings release. Revenue rose 4 percent to $68.3 billion, while profit excluding notable items climbed to $36.6 billion from $34.2 billion, underscoring the health of the bank's underlying operations.

item.title: Asian stocks climb as Wall Street tech rebound eases AI fears
item.description:
Asian markets opened higher on Wednesday as a tech-driven rebound on Wall Street eased fears about the disruptive effects of artificial intelligence that had rattled global equities earlier in the week. The gains came ahead of Nvidia's closely watched quarterly earnings report, due later Wednesday, and as investors digested President Donald Trump's State of the Union address delivered Tuesday evening.

The MSCI Asia Pacific Index extended its advance to a third consecutive day, according to Bloomberg, with shares rising across Japan, South Korea, and Australia. Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed around 1% in early trading, while South Korea's Kospi also gained approximately 1%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 opened nearly 1% higher. In mainland China, the Shanghai Composite rose for a second straight session, climbing about 0.5%, with technology and AI-related stocks leading the advance.

item.title: Study: climate policies averted 3B tons of CO2 in 2022
item.description:
Countries that adopt stricter and better-targeted climate policies are cutting carbon emissions faster, according to what researchers describe as the most comprehensive analysis of global climate policy ever assembled. The study, published Monday in Nature Communications, analyzed more than 3,900 policies enacted since 2000 across 43 leading economies responsible for more than three-quarters of global emissions.

By comparing present-day emissions with a scenario in which no climate policies existed, the international research team found that existing policies avoided an estimated 3.1 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2022 alone — roughly equal to the European Union's entire annual output.

item.title: Study links Saturn's rings to ancient crash that formed Titan
item.description: Saturn's largest moon, Titan, and its spectacular ring system may both owe their existence to a single cataclysmic event — a collision between two ancient moons roughly 400 million years ago, according to a study led by SETI Institute scientist Matija Ćuk. The research, posted to the preprint server arXiv on February 11 and accepted for publication in The Planetary Science Journal, presents computer simulations suggesting the crash reshaped much of the Saturnian system.

item.title: Study finds 40,000-year-old carvings approach complexity of earliest writing
item.description: More than 40,000 years ago, Ice Age humans in Europe were carving patterns of dots, lines, and crosses into tools and ivory figurines — and a new study finds those markings were far from random. A computational analysis of more than 3,000 such symbols, published this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), concludes that the engravings display a level of complexity and information density comparable to proto-cuneiform, the earliest known writing system that emerged in Mesopotamia around 3,000 B.C.E. The findings arrive alongside a separate study, published in Science Advances, that pushes the oldest known Homo erectus fossils in eastern Asia back to 1.77 million years ago. Together, the two papers reshape longstanding assumptions about when early humans began encoding information and how rapidly our ancestors spread across the globe.

item.title: Oil holds near 7-month highs ahead of US-Iran talks
item.description:
Oil prices hovered near their highest levels in seven months on Tuesday as markets braced for a critical round of nuclear talks between the United States and Iran, with traders weighing the risk of a military conflict that could disrupt crude supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures climbed as high as $72.50 a barrel on Monday — the highest since July 31 — before settling around $71.40, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures touched $67.28, their highest since August 4, according to Reuters. Both benchmarks held near those levels in early Wednesday trading in Asia, with Brent rising 0.64% to $71.22 and WTI gaining 0.6% to $66.05.

item.title: General Atlantic stake sale values ByteDance at $550B
item.description:
Investment firm General Atlantic is selling a stake in ByteDance in a deal that values the Chinese social media giant at $550 billion, according to a Reuters exclusive citing two people with knowledge of the matter. The proposed transaction would be the first major share sale since the Trump administration cleared the divestiture of TikTok's U.S. operations in January, and it marks a dramatic rise in the privately held company's valuation.

The $550 billion figure represents a 66% jump from an employee share buyback last year that priced ByteDance at more than $330 billion, and a 15% increase from a secondary market transaction in November that valued the company at $480 billion.

item.title: Shrinking sea ice threatens emperor penguins during moult, study finds
item.description:
Scientists studying satellite images of Antarctica have stumbled upon the first-ever observation of emperor penguin moulting colonies — and with it, a troubling new dimension to the species' struggle for survival. The discovery, published Wednesday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, reveals that shrinking sea ice is forcing the birds into increasingly crowded groups during their annual feather replacement, with potentially fatal consequences.

The findings from the British Antarctic Survey add to a growing body of evidence that climate change is pushing the world's largest penguin species toward extinction. At current rates of warming, there is a 45% chance the species will disappear by the end of the century, the survey said.

item.title: Japan's Nikkei closes at all-time high as AI rally lifts global markets
item.description: Markets around the world climbed on Wednesday, with Japan's Nikkei 225 closing at an all-time high and Europe's STOXX 600 touching a record, as a Wall Street rally fueled by renewed optimism about artificial intelligence rippled across global exchanges.
